title: To a parent whose child has stopped believing
note: An open letter from this site, written in its own voice. It is not a letter from a reader, and the reader it addresses is not a real person: it is written to anyone in this situation.
body:
Dear parent,

You may have found out by accident: a prayer quietly missed for months, a remark at dinner, a browser left open. Or your child may have told you, which took more courage than either of you will say out loud. However it came, you are probably frightened, and you may be ashamed of being frightened. Both are what love feels like when it does not know what to do.

Before anything else, the most important thing you can do this week is to make sure your child knows they are still yours. Not on condition. Not once they come back. Now. A young person who loses their faith and their family in the same month has lost too much to think clearly about either.

It may help to know what doubt usually is. It is very rarely a decision made lightly or out of spite. More often it is a question that grew because no one could be asked it safely: about a verse, about suffering, about something a teacher did, about why the people who spoke loudest for the religion behaved as they did. Questions grow in the dark. They shrink, or at least become manageable, in the light.

So ask, and then listen for longer than is comfortable. What happened? What did you read? What is the part that will not let you go? You do not need to have an answer ready, and you should not pretend to one you do not have. "I do not know, but I would like to find out with you" is an honest answer, and honesty is worth more to them at this moment than a quick reply.

Do not threaten. Do not shame them in front of relatives, and do not hand them to someone who will. Pressure can produce a person who prays in front of you and nowhere else, and that is not what you want for them. The Qur'an says there is no compulsion in religion (2:256), and it tells the Prophet himself that he cannot guide whom he loves (28:56). If that was true for him, it is true for us, and there is a strange relief in it. Their heart is not yours to force. It is yours to keep open.

Look after yourself as well. Talk to someone you trust who will not spread it. If there is fear in your home, of anger or of what the wider family might do, take that seriously and get help early.

The doubts on this site are written for the questions children carry, and you are welcome to read them first, or together. Whatever your child decides, a door that stays open is the thing they will remember.

With every good wish for you both,

Murtadd

title: To someone who has just left
note: An open letter from this site, written in its own voice. It is not a letter from a reader, and the reader it addresses is not a real person: it is written to anyone in this situation.
body:
Dear friend,

If you have just left Islam, or are standing at the edge of it, you may be feeling several things at once: relief, grief, anger, fear, and a loneliness that is hard to describe to anyone who has not felt it. You may also be bracing for a letter like this one to try to change your mind. It will not try. That is your decision to make, in your own time, and no one can make it for you.

What we would like to say is simpler. You are still a person worth caring about, whatever you now believe, and you deserve to be safe.

Safety comes first. In some families and some countries, leaving carries real risk. If you are in danger, contact your local emergency services or a helpline now, before anything else. Think carefully about who you tell, and when. There is no duty to announce anything to anyone before you are ready, and being careful is not the same as being dishonest.

Then, if you can, be gentle with the people who loved you inside the faith. Many of them will react with fear before they find their way to anything else. Fear can sound like anger. Sometimes it softens with time, and sometimes it does not, but it is worth leaving room for the first.

Be gentle with yourself, too. A change this large takes time to settle, and it is normal for it to come back in waves: at Eid, at a funeral, at the call to prayer heard from a window. Grieving what you have left does not mean you were wrong to leave, and missing it does not mean you must return. Both feelings can be true at once.

You may have left because of an argument, or because of how you were treated, or both. If it was the treatment, we are sorry. What was done to you was not owed to you, and it was not the religion speaking. If it was an argument, this site tries to state such arguments fairly and answer them on the evidence. You are welcome to read with as much suspicion as you like. You are equally welcome not to read at all.

And if one day you have a question you would like to put to someone who will not pressure you, the contact form is there. No one here will treat it as a contest.

Wishing you safety and peace,

Murtadd

title: To a convert who feels let down
note: An open letter from this site, written in its own voice. It is not a letter from a reader, and the reader it addresses is not a real person: it is written to anyone in this situation.
body:
Dear friend,

You came to Islam with your whole heart, and somewhere along the way the community that welcomed you at your shahada stopped answering the phone. Perhaps you were celebrated for a month and then left alone for Ramadan. Perhaps you were told your clothes, your name, your music and your family were all wrong, by people who never asked about any of them. Perhaps you were made to feel like a project, or a trophy, or a guest who had stayed too long.

If any of that is your story, we are sorry. It should not have happened, and it is not a small thing. Many who come to the faith as adults give up a great deal to do it, and they are owed better than enthusiasm followed by silence.

It may help to separate two things that the disappointment has tied together. One is the question of whether what you came to believe is true. The other is how some Muslims behaved towards you. They are different questions, and the second does not answer the first. The Prophet's community was not built of people born into it; it was built of people who came to it, and the Qur'an judges a person by their taqwa (49:13), whatever their birth or lineage. Those who treated you as less were measuring by a standard the religion does not use.

That does not oblige you to stay. Your doubts may be about the beliefs themselves, and if so they deserve a real answer. This site tries to give real answers, and to concede where a concession is honest.

But if what you are carrying is mostly loneliness, please do not carry it alone. Look for one or two people, not a crowd: someone who will eat with you, ask how you are, and not correct your pronunciation. They are there, though they are rarely the loudest people in the room. And keep your own family close. Nothing in the faith asks you to give them up, and the Qur'an asks you to keep kindness with parents even across a difference of belief (31:15).

Whatever you decide, you are not a failed project. You are a person who took a serious question seriously, and that is to your credit.

With respect and warm wishes,

Murtadd

title: To someone afraid to say it out loud
note: An open letter from this site, written in its own voice. It is not a letter from a reader, and the reader it addresses is not a real person: it is written to anyone in this situation.
body:
Dear friend,

There is a question you have not said out loud. Perhaps you typed it into a search box late at night and closed the window straight afterwards. Perhaps you have been carrying it for years. You may be afraid of what it means about you, or of what would happen if anyone knew.

First: having a question does not make you a bad person, and it does not make you a hypocrite. Doubt is not the same as disbelief, and wondering is not the same as deciding. Many people of deep faith have passed through exactly where you are standing.

Second: you do not have to resolve it tonight. A question this large is not answered in one sitting, and a mind that is exhausted and frightened is not in a good state to answer anything. Sleep. Eat. Go for a walk. The question will still be there in the morning, and you will be better able to look at it.

Third: you are allowed to look at it properly. That means reading the strongest form of the objection, not a caricature of it, and then reading the evidence on the other side with the same care. It means checking sources rather than trusting whoever sounds most certain. The Start Here page offers three ways in, depending on what kind of question you are carrying.

Fourth: if the question has come with something heavier, a feeling that you cannot go on, or a fear for your safety, please put the question down for now and talk to someone today. Contact your local emergency services or a helpline in your country. Your life matters more than any argument, in either direction.

Whatever you conclude in the end, you deserve to reach it honestly, without being rushed, shamed or frightened into it. That is what this site is for.

With care,

Murtadd
